## Eight practitioner assumptions, negated

| # | Common assumption | If it were false, the conditional effect would be… |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | A conv's gain on a deep-chain edge doesn't depend on whether a shortcut exists elsewhere. | Deep-chain convs gain more with a 0→3 identity shortcut, which acts as a residual and eases optimization. They gain less when 0→3 already carries a conv, because that capacity is already supplied. |
| A2 | Convs on parallel edges into the same node add up roughly additively. | Parallel convs into one node are redundant, so each one's marginal gain shrinks. |
| A3 | Parameter-free ops (skip, pool) are near-neutral "glue" whatever their neighbours are. | Skip next to or around a conv acts as a residual and becomes much more valuable. Pooling stacked with pooling blurs features and becomes harmful. |
| A4 | Removing an edge costs about the same regardless of which other routes survive. | Removing an edge hurts less when a parallel conv route substitutes for it. It hurts more when the remaining route is only pooling. |
| A5 | Receptive field is never saturated in a 4-node cell, so a 3×3 helps equally everywhere. | Edge-5 3×3 helps more when the inputs to node 2 do little spatial mixing (skip or pool). It helps less when they are already 3×3. |
| A6 | 1×1 convs are a weaker but interchangeable substitute for 3×3. | A 1×1 is a channel mixer whose value depends on spatial features upstream. Chained 1×1s with no spatial mixing are especially poor. |
| A7 | An edge's importance doesn't depend on node fan-in. | When an edge is the sole input to a node, it is a bottleneck, so upgrading it matters more. |
| A8 | Effects found on 32×32 CIFAR transfer unchanged to 16×16 ImageNet16-120. | Spatial ops saturate sooner on 16×16 inputs. The interactions listed above should still hold in sign, just with different magnitude. |
